name: Ama
tagline: An AI assistant pitched as an agent that does the work for you rather than just chatting about it.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The general shape of this category is very cheap to rebuild: a chat loop, a model API key, some document ingestion, a few tools the model can call. An agent can absolutely get you a local assistant that answers over your own files and runs a small set of actions in one sitting. What does not fall out of a one-shot build is the part that makes an assistant feel like a product: the connectors into the places your work actually lives, the prompt scaffolding that stops the agent wandering off, and a client you can reach from your phone. Public detail on this specific product is thin, so treat the verdict as a read on the category rather than a line-by-line teardown. If your use is "ask questions about my own stuff and occasionally do a thing", the DIY version is real; if you wanted it wired into your calendar, inbox and tools, you are signing up for a long tail of OAuth work.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a local chat assistant that ingests your files, answers with citations, and can call a handful of tools you define.
requirements: An LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic) in .env
Local disk for the SQLite store and uploaded files
Willingness to write your own tool functions for anything beyond search and fetch
whatYouLose: Connectors: calendar, email, Slack, Drive, whatever else, each one its own OAuth slog
A mobile or desktop client, so your assistant lives on localhost only
Someone else's prompt and retrieval tuning, which is most of why hosted assistants feel competent
Voice, background jobs, notifications and anything else that makes an assistant proactive
Model upgrades happening without you noticing or caring
moatNotes: Assistant products win on the boring plumbing into your existing accounts, not on the chat box.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a chat box over your own files is a demo, and an assistant that can actually see your calendar, your inbox and your documents without you writing four OAuth flows is a product. People pay for the connectors, the reliability when the model misbehaves, and being able to use the thing from a phone at a bus stop. The DIY version is genuinely useful for a single person with a folder of documents, and genuinely annoying the moment you want it to touch anything else you own.
notes: The chat loop is a weekend, the integrations are a career.
prompt:
Build a local-only personal AI assistant. No accounts, no cloud services beyond one model API, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind, single app, run with npm run dev
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for messages, documents and embedding chunks
- Anthropic or OpenAI SDK, key read from .env.local as MODEL_API_KEY and MODEL_PROVIDER
- No auth, no user table, this runs on 127.0.0.1 for one person

Features in scope:
1. Chat UI with streaming responses, persistent conversation list in the sidebar, rename and delete conversations.
2. File ingestion: drag in .txt, .md and .pdf, chunk to roughly 800 tokens with overlap, embed, store vectors as BLOBs in SQLite, cosine similarity in plain JS. No vector database.
3. Retrieval: on each message, pull the top 8 chunks, inject them into the system prompt, and render clickable source citations under the answer.
4. Tool calling with exactly three tools: search_documents, fetch_url (plain text extraction), and run_calculation. Show each tool call and its result inline in the transcript as a collapsible block.
5. A settings page to edit the system prompt and the model name, stored in SQLite.
6. A memory table: let the user pin short facts that get prepended to every system prompt, with an edit and delete UI.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile app, OAuth to any third party, multi-user, voice input, background jobs, hosted deployment, Docker.

Deliverables: working app, schema created on first run via a migrate script, seed script that ingests any files in ./corpus, and a README with setup in under ten lines. Commit .env.example, never a real key.
